{{Short description|Mathematical school in Ancient Greece}}

'''The School of Chios''' ({{langx|grc|Σχολή της Χίου}}) was a mathematical school in [[ancient Greece]] that flourished from around 480 BC to 450 BC.

== Main Representatives of the School ==
The School of Chios was a mathematical school established in the early 5th century, succeeding the [[Pythagoreanism|Pythagorean School]]. Its most prominent representative was [[Hippocrates of Chios]] (~470-400 BC), who flourished around 440 BC. His teacher was [[Oenopides|Oenopides of Chios]], who was a generation older. Also, [[Anaxagoras]] (500-428 BC) was likely a member of the School. <ref>S. X. Goudouvas (2015), pp.30-32</ref>

== The Mathematical Work of the School ==
There is no information on whether the School of Chios was based in [[Chios]] or if its representatives hailed from there. However, it was the brief period between the Pythagorean School and the [[Platonic Academy]]. The Academy declined, and its traces were lost shortly after the mid-5th century, during a flourishing geometric tradition, where the central focus was on the three famous "unsolvable" problems of antiquity: the [[Doubling the cube|Doubling of the cube]] or Delian problem, the Trisection of the angle, and the [[Squaring the circle|Squaring of the circle]]. <ref>S. X. Goudouvas (2015), pp.30-32 & Van der Waerden (2003), pp. 146-147</ref>

Anaxagoras is mentioned as the first to deal with the problem of squaring the circle. <ref>S. X. Goudouvas (2015), p.130</ref>

According to [[Proclus]], Oenopides was involved in mathematics and gained fame from it; he also introduced the use of the rule and compass for geometric constructions. <ref>S. X. Goudouvas (2015), p.30</ref>

Hippocrates is mentioned as the first to reduce the problem of doubling the cube to its equivalent, the interpolation of two mean proportionals between two straight line segments a and b=2a, so that the continuous proportions a/x=x/y=y/2a hold. Hippocrates also squared lunules, according to Simplicius (4th century AD), in a text that is preserved to us. <ref>S. X. Goudouvas (2015), pp.31</ref>

The peak of the School of Chios did not last long, and the scientific center soon after the mid-5th century BC shifted to [[Ancient Athens|Athens]]. The three above-mentioned main representatives of the School of Chios settled in Athens and continued their mathematical work.
